content: A study conducted in Cameroon, Côte d’Ivoire, Eswatini, Kenya, Lesotho, Mozambique, Rwanda, and Zimbabwe involved structured interviews with healthcare workers providing infant testing services and semi-structured interviews with national and regional laboratory managers or early infant diagnosis program managers. These interviews were conducted both before and after the implementation of point-of-care infant testing. Healthcare workers reported that point-of-care infant testing was easy to use, with 74% stating it was very simple to perform the test. Additionally, 93% of healthcare workers expressed high satisfaction with the rapid turnaround time and the ability to initiate treatment for infants living with HIV more quickly. Access to high-quality diagnostic testing should be continuously expanded to address HIV and other molecular testing needs. Ideally, this should involve integrating laboratory-based and point-of-care technologies within a cohesive laboratory network. Establishing a broad network of decentralized specimen collection and/or point-of-care testing requires centralized support from national laboratories and programs. This support is essential to ensure adequate training, mentorship, service and maintenance, continuous quality assurance, and accurate data entry at the point of care. Expanding human resource capacity is also critical for decentralizing specimen collection and task sharing. In some countries, legal and regulatory frameworks and policies may need to be adjusted to enable non-laboratory personnel to participate in specimen collection and testing. Concurrently, scaling up and strengthening human resource capacity, including laboratory personnel, will be vital for expanding diagnostic access. The World Health Organization (WHO) has developed tools and guidelines for human resources in health and recommends a systematic approach to addressing health workforce dynamics. This includes assessing workload indicators among healthcare providers. Additional diagnostic accuracy studies comparing the performance of newer point-of-care technologies (for infant diagnosis and viral load testing) between non-laboratory personnel and laboratory professionals would be valuable. Decentralization of antiretroviral therapy (ART) care should be considered as a strategy to increase access and improve retention in care. Effective approaches include initiating ART in hospitals with maintenance at peripheral health facilities, initiating and maintaining ART in peripheral health facilities, and initiating ART at peripheral health facilities with maintenance at the community level. Community-level care includes external outreach sites, health posts, home-based services, or community-based organizations. The frequency of clinic visits should depend on the patient’s health status. The rapid scale-up of ART programs has posed significant challenges to health systems in high HIV burden settings with limited resources. Many clinics experience long waiting times due to the high volume of patients requiring care. Decentralizing HIV care and treatment has been shown to reduce waiting times and bring services closer to patients’ homes. It also strengthens community engagement by linking community-based interventions with health facilities, optimizing access to services, care-seeking behavior, and retention in care. A systematic review identified 16 studies demonstrating that decentralizing ART care, either from hospitals to health centers or from health centers to community-based care, reduces attrition without compromising clinical outcomes. Most of these studies were conducted in sub-Saharan Africa, and the benefits of decentralization may vary by setting. The optimal model for ART decentralization depends on the local context, including the burden of HIV infection and the healthcare delivery system. Programs should determine which clinical and laboratory services will be available at each level of the healthcare delivery system. Program managers should consider patient preferences, the number of people likely to attend decentralized settings, and whether decentralization brings services closer to those who would otherwise travel long distances for ART. Decentralization should be accompanied by efforts to strengthen linkage and referral systems. Community-based treatment programs should be linked with care at health facilities and supported by adequate laboratory, diagnostic, monitoring, evaluation, and supply management systems. Standards of care should be defined for each level of the health system, including the private sector. The role of each level should align with its capacity, and lines of authority and accountability should be clear and well understood. In many settings, decentralizing ART requires task sharing to ensure an appropriate mix of healthcare workers at peripheral facilities. An appropriate regulatory framework (laws, regulations, policies, and guidelines) is needed to enable tasks to be performed by different cadres of healthcare workers. Adaptations may be necessary for specific populations. HIV care and treatment services for pregnant and postpartum women, as well as HIV-exposed and infected children, can be provided in decentralized settings. This is a preferred option in high HIV burden settings where many women and children access health services in primary care settings. In low HIV burden settings, a centralized service delivery model with community linkage may be more appropriate. Some groups, such as adolescents and key populations, may prefer to receive HIV services in facilities not close to their homes due to stigma and concerns about disclosure. In such cases, healthcare providers should incorporate the values and preferences of these populations when designing service delivery models. Chronic care requires integrating and linking related services to ensure comprehensive and consistent care over time. This includes providing related services in the same settings, establishing systems to share information, and ensuring effective referrals across settings and providers. Integrating and linking services can reduce missed opportunities for initiating ART, enhance adherence support, and optimize retention in care. In generalized epidemic settings, ART should be initiated and maintained in pregnant and postpartum women and infants within maternal and child healthcare settings, with linkage and referral to ongoing HIV care and ART as appropriate. Since 2016, WHO has recommended initiating ART for everyone living with HIV, regardless of CD4 cell count, including pregnant and breastfeeding women. However, access to ART for these populations remains a challenge, as does providing essential HIV services to HIV-exposed uninfected and infected infants and ensuring that services for preventing mother-to-child transmission reach vulnerable groups such as pregnant adolescent girls, young women, female sex workers, and women who inject drugs. Maternal and child health settings provide a critical opportunity to offer ART, as many women living with HIV only access health services during pregnancy. In most generalized HIV epidemic settings, maternal and child health services are provided at the primary care level, where pregnant women and children predominantly access health services. WHO recommends offering HIV testing services to pregnant women through provider-initiated approaches as an essential component of maternal, newborn, and child health services. Couple and partner HIV testing is also recommended for all pregnant women and their partners in generalized HIV epidemics and should be considered for key populations in concentrated and low-level epidemics. In high HIV burden settings, retesting is advised for all pregnant women with an unknown or HIV-negative status during late pregnancy (third trimester). Catch-up testing is needed if the first test or retest is missed or delayed. Countries with a high HIV burden could consider an additional retest in the postpartum period for specific districts or regions with high HIV burden or incidence, women from key populations, and women with partners living with HIV who do not have suppressed viral loads. ART should be available in maternal and child health clinics or easily accessible through a linked model of service delivery. Countries with generalized epidemics may consider a phased approach to providing ART in maternal and child health settings, prioritizing facilities with the largest HIV burden and building health systems to ensure uninterrupted ART, good adherence, and retention to maintain viral suppression. All pregnant women, regardless of when they start ART, may require more intensive monitoring of viral suppression, including viral load testing at 34–36 weeks of gestation (or at the latest at delivery) to identify women at risk of treatment failure and/or delivering infants at higher risk of perinatal transmission. Additionally, a viral load test is recommended for all breastfeeding women three months after delivery and every six months thereafter to detect viremic episodes during the postnatal period. Not all maternal and child health settings will have the capacity to provide long-term HIV care and treatment for women, their partners, and infants. These settings will need to assess and decide on the best time for transitioning and linking mothers and their infants to chronic HIV care and from chronic care into maternal and child health settings when the pregnant woman was already receiving ART at the time of conception. Providing choice for where a woman living with HIV receives ART care remains important and should not interfere with the efficient provision of quality and person-centered antenatal care. Factors to consider in the assessment include the capacity and quality of HIV care in the maternal and child health-care setting, the acceptability and proximity of alternative HIV care settings, and the burden of HIV infection. In settings with a high burden of HIV and tuberculosis (TB), ART should be initiated in TB treatment settings, with linkage to ongoing HIV care and ART. TB treatment may also be provided for people living with HIV in HIV care settings if they have been diagnosed with TB. Since 2010, WHO has recommended ART for everyone with TB who is living with HIV, regardless of CD4 cell count. In 2021, WHO recommended initiating ART as soon as possible and within two weeks after starting TB treatment. Co-trimoxazole prophylaxis is also recommended for all people with both TB and HIV. TB infection control measures are crucial in HIV care settings to minimize the risk of nosocomial transmission of TB. A systematic review evaluating the effectiveness of delivering ART in TB treatment settings identified 19 observational studies, many of which showed increased uptake and timeliness of ART initiation. However, data on mortality and TB treatment success were inconsistent. The same review identified five observational studies evaluating the effectiveness of delivering TB treatment in HIV care settings. Two studies reported decreased mortality, and another showed comparable mortality rates. Sexual and reproductive health services, including contraception, can be integrated within HIV care settings. Evidence indicates that sex workers have a greater unmet need for contraception than the general population and often rely excessively on condoms alone instead of the recommended dual protection. Globally, the proportion of the need for sexual and reproductive health services satisfied by modern methods was 76% in 2019, but this fell to less than 50% in western and central Africa. WHO emphasizes the importance of linking sexual and reproductive health and rights with HIV services for adolescent girls and young women. Women living with HIV face unique challenges and human rights violations related to their sexuality and reproduction within their families, communities, and healthcare institutions. Creating an enabling environment is especially emphasized to support more effective health interventions and better health outcomes.
